terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: Compares an industry's share of local employment or sales with its share nationally — local share ÷ national share — so 1.0 marks a perfectly typical market, above about 1.25 says the activity is concentrated here and likely serves customers beyond it, and below about 0.75 says local demand is being met from somewhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: Situation-analysis questions supply local and national employment figures and expect the ratio read against 1.0; it is how a plan defends choosing one metro over another with evidence rather than preference.

terms.definition: A dependency network that estimates each task's expected duration as optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic, divided by six — a weighted three-point estimate for work with uncertain durations, unlike a critical path calculation, which assumes one fixed duration per task.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you three time estimates for a task and ask for the expected duration; the weighted formula, not a plain average of the three numbers, is the scored answer.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: Having just done or displayed something creditable makes the next questionable act easier, because the earlier one buys credit against the self-image. It runs opposite to the intuition that good behavior predicts more good behavior: participants who first endorsed a minority candidate afterward favored a white applicant more readily than participants given no chance to establish credentials, so the good act enabled the biased one.
terms.whyItMatters: In an ethics case where a firm cites its diversity award or its donation record while defending a questionable decision, naming the licensing pattern turns a weak 'that is irrelevant' into the analysis a judge scores; it also warns against recommending a visible ethics gesture as the whole remedy.

terms.definition: A pre-release trial run by the developer's own employees inside a controlled company setting, so defects are found before any outsider sees the product; beta testing hands the same build to real customers in their own environment, which makes who runs it and where the dividing line between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: Development-stage exam items list a testing activity and ask which stage it belongs to; the answer turns entirely on whether outsiders are involved.

terms.definition: Repricing protection for preferred holders when a later round prices below theirs. A full ratchet resets their conversion price all the way to the new low price no matter how few shares were sold; a broad-based weighted average blends the old and new prices in proportion to shares issued, so it takes far less from the founders.
terms.whyItMatters: In a term-negotiation roleplay the two forms look interchangeable on paper and are not: naming which one you would accept, and why the weighted-average form protects the common stock, is what separates a top score.

terms.definition: The combination of hardware, software, data, and people used to collect, process, store, and share information.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding systems is key when competitors evaluate technology investments.

terms.definition: Fits the line y = a + bx through the observations so the slope b estimates how much the outcome moves per one-unit change in the driver, letting a finding be stated as each extra $1,000 of local ad spend adding 62 units; a correlation coefficient reports only how tight the relationship is and yields no rate of change to plan with.
terms.whyItMatters: Turning research into a recommendation a manager can budget against needs the slope, which is why forecasting prompts reach for this rather than a correlation.

terms.definition: Disagreement between channel members over goals, territories, or profits.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict damages efficiency; resolving it is key to long-term channel health.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring lenders to disclose the annual percentage rate, finance charge and total payments in a standard form before a consumer signs.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why two loan offers in a roleplay can be compared at all, and why a lender quoting only a monthly payment is out of compliance.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: A horizontal bar timeline showing each task's start, duration and overlap against calendar dates; it displays schedule but not logic, whereas a PERT network draws the dependency arrows that reveal which tasks actually control the finish date.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-management roleplays ask which tool to bring to a status meeting: the bar timeline communicates progress to a client, but it cannot answer which delay pushes the deadline.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: The wages, salaries, bonuses, and other financial rewards given for work.
terms.whyItMatters: Fair, competitive pay attracts talent, motivates performance, and aids retention.

terms.definition: The specific benefit that makes a product distinctly better than rivals'.
terms.whyItMatters: A clear USP gives customers a compelling reason to choose the product.

terms.definition: A basic first version of a product used to test demand and gather feedback.
terms.whyItMatters: An MVP validates an idea cheaply before heavy development.

terms.definition: A written table stating how long each class of record is kept and when it must be destroyed, built on statutory floors rather than preference: the IRS's ordinary three-year assessment window, seven years for records supporting a bad-debt or worthless-securities claim, and the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that audit work papers survive seven years.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-records roleplay asks how long the storeroom keeps signed invoices before shredding them, and a judge expects a statutory minimum, not a guess like 'a few years'.

terms.definition: Concluding that a difference is real when it is not, the false positive that a 0.05 significance threshold knowingly accepts about 5% of the time; the mirror-image mistake of missing a difference that genuinely exists is a Type II error, and tightening the threshold to cut the risk of one necessarily raises the risk of the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Deciding whether a test result justifies a full rollout, the tested judgment is what it costs to be wrong in each direction, not just whether the number cleared 0.05.

terms.definition: A merchant wholesaler that owns the merchandise sitting on a retailer's fixture, chooses the assortment, sets the planogram, restocks on its own route, and is paid only for units that actually scan — so the retailer risks nothing but the floor space. A conventional wholesaler is the opposite arrangement: it bills the retailer at delivery and the retailer owns the unsold goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Convenience-store, greeting-card and paperback scenarios use this to test who bears shrink and markdown risk when the supplier still owns the stock on the shelf.

terms.definition: State-granted legal permission to perform work that is illegal without it — signing an audit opinion, selling securities, practicing law. A voluntary certification is issued by a private association instead, so losing it costs you the letters after your name but never the legal right to keep working.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay that asks what a new hire may and may not sign turns on this line: an unlicensed staff accountant can prepare the workpapers but cannot issue the opinion.

terms.definition: An arrangement where a manufacturer reimburses part of a retailer's local advertising cost, usually on the condition that the ad features the manufacturer's brand and follows its format and logo rules, with reimbursement accrued against the retailer's purchase volume.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail roleplay where the store cannot afford a campaign alone is solved by claiming these funds, and the competitor is expected to name the strings attached rather than treat the money as unrestricted.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: Summing durations along every dependency chain and taking the longest one as the shortest possible project duration; every task on it has zero float, so any slip there slips the whole project, while a delay off it is absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A project roleplay that asks which of several late tasks to escalate is answered by locating the zero-float chain, because effort spent on the others buys no finish-date improvement.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: Separations during a period divided by average headcount for that period, times 100 — 18 departures against an average of 120 staff gives 15% — and the voluntary portion is tracked separately because it, not the involuntary portion, signals a retention problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Management roleplays open with a turnover figure and expect you to compute or interpret it and split voluntary from involuntary before recommending a fix.

terms.definition: The first 2.5% of a market to buy something new -- venturesome, able to absorb a failed purchase, and often socially outside the mainstream, which limits their influence; the early adopters who follow are the next 13.5% and carry the opinion leadership that actually moves the majority.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target at launch; quoting the 2.5% band and then explaining why that group cannot spread adoption alone is what separates the top scores.

terms.definition: Allows holders of a specified majority — often a majority of the preferred stock — to force minority shareholders to vote for an approved sale and sell on identical terms, preventing a small holder from blocking an exit. Its mirror image, the tag-along right, instead lets a minority holder demand inclusion in someone else's sale.
terms.whyItMatters: An exit-planning roleplay where one early shareholder refuses to sell turns on whether this clause exists; a competitor who confuses it with the tag-along gives the minority holder a veto that the documents never granted.

terms.definition: An instruction that suspends the retention schedule and freezes every document touching anticipated or filed litigation, overriding routine destruction until counsel lifts it; skipping it exposes the company to spoliation sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) even when the deletion was only the ordinary schedule running as designed.
terms.whyItMatters: In a legal-issues roleplay where a customer has threatened suit, the first correct action is stopping automatic email deletion — not gathering documents after the subpoena arrives.

terms.definition: Creating clear, unbiased questions that collect reliable data.
terms.whyItMatters: Good design yields valid data; poor design introduces error.

terms.definition: A wholesaler that TAKES TITLE to a shipment but never physically handles it — it sells the load, then instructs the producer to ship straight to the buyer, collecting the margin between the two prices. That title-without-possession position is what separates it from a broker, which never takes title at all, and from a full-service wholesaler, which warehouses and delivers the goods itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Bulk-commodity channel questions test whether you see that this member is legally the seller of record and therefore liable on the sale, even though it never touched the freight.

terms.definition: Deals won divided by every qualified opportunity worked in the period — 15 wins out of 60 qualified opportunities is 25%. The denominator keeps opportunities that are still open or that ended in no decision, which is exactly what win rate throws out, so this figure always reads lower than win rate for the same rep.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales-management roleplay that asks you to diagnose a rep whose revenue is falling, a dropping close rate against a steady win rate points at unqualified prospecting rather than weak closing technique.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: A deliverable-oriented decomposition of a project into progressively smaller work packages governed by the 100 percent rule — the children of any element must sum to exactly that element, no more and no less — so it captures scope, not sequence, which the schedule adds afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how to start planning a project, the accepted first move is decomposing deliverables before estimating or scheduling, and the completeness rule is what stops forgotten work becoming a budget overrun.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: Using prices like $9.99 to shape customer perception of value.
terms.whyItMatters: It shows how price presentation affects customer behavior and sales.

terms.definition: The 13.5% of buyers who follow the innovators -- respected opinion leaders inside the mainstream whose endorsement decides whether an item reaches the 34% early majority; innovators, the first 2.5%, buy sooner but sit too far outside the group to persuade it.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion plans for a launch are scored on targeting the group that others watch; naming the 13.5% band and its opinion-leader role answers the indicator directly.

terms.definition: A major shift in a venture's direction, product, or market based on feedback.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurs must adapt and justify course corrections when assumptions fail.

terms.definition: A systematic review of external conditions, competitor activity, and market trends.
terms.whyItMatters: Scanning the environment lets competitors spot opportunities and threats before deciding.

terms.definition: Whether an instrument truly measures the abstract idea it claims to, so a three-item loyalty battery may in fact be capturing nothing but recent convenience; this is a separate question from reliability, which only asks whether repeated administrations agree, and a broken thermometer reading 50 every single time is perfectly reliable and completely invalid.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing whether a proposed study will actually answer the business question, this is the distinction a judge listens for when a competitor defends an instrument.

terms.definition: A non-competing business that partners to offer complementary products to shared customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Affinity partnerships extend reach and value without adding intermediaries.

terms.definition: A one-page diagram placing the unwanted event at the center, its causes fanning left and its consequences fanning right, with preventive controls and mitigating controls drawn as barriers on each side, showing at a glance where a single barrier is carrying far too much weight.
terms.whyItMatters: It gives a risk presentation a visual a non-technical owner can follow, which is often what earns the communication points in a risk-management roleplay.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: Latest allowable start minus earliest possible start for a task — the delay it can absorb before the project finish moves; total float is shared along a chain, whereas free float is the smaller amount that delays no immediately following task at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a network with early and late start dates, exam questions ask how long a task can slip; confusing the shared allowance with the task-level one over-promises the client in a status roleplay.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: A defense to copyright infringement weighed on the four statutory factors of 17 U.S.C. section 107: the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is transformative or commercial; the nature of the copyrighted work; the amount and substantiality of the portion taken; and the effect on the potential market for the original. No factor is decisive and there is no safe word count or percentage, though the market-effect factor usually carries the most weight.
terms.whyItMatters: IP-protection roleplays about quoting a rival's review or reusing its product photo in a comparison ad are argued factor by factor.

terms.definition: Measures how closely the lines relate in production, distribution, and end use -- something neither width nor depth can show: two firms each carrying 4 lines and 40 items differ sharply when one sells only refrigerated foods through grocers and the other sells food, tires, and insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification questions ask whether a proposed line fits; the scoring point is that the new line shares plants or channels with the existing ones, not that it sounds related.

terms.definition: Total sales and marketing spend over a period divided by the number of new customers it produced, with salaries, agency fees and tools counted in — not ad spend alone. Blended figures divide by every new customer including organic ones; paid figures count only customers from paid channels and always read higher.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-spend roleplay gives you a monthly budget and a customer count and asks whether the channel is working; the judge expects the division shown and the blended-versus-paid distinction stated out loud.

terms.definition: Swapping direct identifiers for tokens while keeping the re-identification key stored separately, which leaves the file still legally personal data under GDPR Article 4(5) and still inside the regulation's reach; true anonymization destroys that key irreversibly, and only then does the data fall out of scope entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics-in-data-mining item asks whether replacing customer names with ID numbers lets a firm share the file freely, and the graded answer is that it does not while the key survives.

terms.definition: A standardized study a research firm runs on its own initiative and then sells to every subscriber in the category, splitting the cost across all of them; proprietary or custom research is commissioned by a single client, answers that client's exact question and stays confidential, so the trade is comparability and low price against fit and exclusivity.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending where a small business should get category data on a tight budget, the scored distinction is why cheap shared data cannot answer a company-specific question.

terms.definition: Performs the whole function set — carries inventory, extends trade credit, delivers, fields a sales force, and merchandises the account — and prices for it, typically working on a 15 to 25 percent gross margin. A limited-service wholesaler strips some of those out (cash-and-carry drops credit and delivery, a truck jobber drops credit) and consequently operates nearer 8 to 12 percent.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-cost questions ask why one supplier quotes a higher landed price than another; the answer is the bundle of functions inside the margin, not inefficiency.

terms.definition: Brown and Levinson's term for any move that damages a hearer's public self-image - a criticism, a refusal, an order, a correction - together with the two repairs speakers use on it. Negative politeness protects the hearer's freedom by hedging and leaving an exit ('if you have a moment, could you possibly...'); positive politeness protects the hearer's need to be liked, using shared identity, praise and in-group language. Choosing the wrong repair is why a technically polite email still lands badly.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay that asks you to correct an employee's work is scored on which softening strategy you choose, not just on the accuracy of the correction.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: Comparing budgeted cost of work actually completed against what was spent and what was planned: cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost, schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and any index below 1.0 signals over budget or behind schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-evaluation items ask whether a project that has spent sixty percent of its budget is in trouble; only the ratio against work completed answers it, and a raw spending percentage does not.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: A purchase for which buyers accept no substitute and will pass closer outlets to reach one brand -- insistence, not preference; a shopping good is one buyers compare on price, quality, and style across several stores and will happily switch brands on to save money.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution questions follow from this classification: specialty goods justify exclusive distribution and few outlets, while shopping goods need enough outlets for comparison to happen.

terms.definition: Months needed to earn back what one customer cost to win: acquisition cost divided by that customer's monthly revenue times gross margin, so a $900 cost against $100 a month at 75% margin repays in twelve months. Unlike the payback period on a capital project, this one recurs with every customer the venture acquires.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay why the venture needs working capital even while growing, the answer is that cash goes out to win a customer months before it comes back — this figure is the size of that gap.

terms.definition: The European rule granting individuals rights of access, correction, portability and erasure over their own data, requiring a documented lawful basis before any processing begins, forcing breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours, and capping fines at the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: An international e-commerce roleplay asks what changes when the site starts shipping to Ireland, and the answer is these specific obligations and their clock, not a general promise of privacy.

terms.definition: A plan outlining the method, variables, population, and analysis for a study.
terms.whyItMatters: Design choices decide whether research answers the business question.

terms.definition: The management of the flow of goods — storage, transportation, and delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: Logistics efficiency drives channel cost, speed, and customer satisfaction.

terms.definition: Blaming an out-group's failures on what its members are like while writing off its successes as luck, special help or an exception -- and reversing both judgments for one's own group. The individual-level attribution error concerns one person; this is its group-level extension, and it is the specific mechanism by which a stereotype survives meeting a counterexample, since the counterexample gets filed away rather than counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on overcoming stereotypes reward naming the filing-as-exception move, and a Human Resources roleplay about a hiring panel that keeps calling qualified candidates from one school 'unusual for their program' is describing this error rather than open prejudice.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.
